questions.title: Kafka Core Concepts
questions.question: What is Apache Kafka and what are its core architectural concepts?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Kafka: distributed event streaming platform — durable, high-throughput, ordered pub/sub
- Topic: named stream of records — like a table in a database
- Partition: each topic divided into ordered partitions — unit of parallelism and ordering
- Offset: position of a record within a partition — consumers track their position
- Broker: Kafka server node — a cluster has multiple brokers
- Producer: publishes records to topics; Consumer: reads records from topics
- Consumer Group: group of consumers sharing work — each partition assigned to one consumer
- Retention: records kept for a configurable duration (default 7 days), not deleted on consumption

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. Unlike a traditional message queue where messages are deleted after consumption, Kafka retains records for a configurable period — usually 7 days — and consumers track their position in the log using offsets. This means you can replay events, have multiple independent consumer groups each reading the same topic, and even replay historical events from the beginning.

Topics are divided into partitions, and partitions are the unit of both ordering and parallelism. Within a partition, records are strictly ordered. Across partitions, there's no ordering guarantee. When you produce a record, you choose a partition — either randomly, by round-robin, or by a key that deterministically maps to a partition. Records with the same key always go to the same partition, which is how you guarantee ordering for related events.

Consumer groups enable parallel consumption. Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer within a group. With three partitions and three consumers in a group, each consumer handles one partition. Adding a fourth consumer leaves one idle — you can't have more active consumers than partitions.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Kafka Architecture

```
Kafka Cluster (3 brokers)
├── Topic: orders (3 partitions)
│   ├── Partition 0: [msg0, msg1, msg4, msg7]
│   ├── Partition 1: [msg2, msg5, msg8]
│   └── Partition 2: [msg3, msg6, msg9]
│
├── Producer: sends messages → partitioner decides which partition
└── Consumer Group "inventory-service"
    ├── Consumer 1 → reads Partition 0
    ├── Consumer 2 → reads Partition 1
    └── Consumer 3 → reads Partition 2
    (3 partitions, 3 consumers: perfect balance)
```

## Key Concepts

| Concept | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| Topic | Named stream (like a log file) |
| Partition | Ordered, immutable sequence within topic |
| Offset | Record's position within partition |
| Producer | Writes records to partitions |
| Consumer | Reads records, tracks offset |
| Consumer Group | Shares partitions for parallel consumption |
| Broker | Kafka server node |
| Replication | Partitions replicated across brokers for fault tolerance |

## Offset Management

```
Partition 0: [msg0] [msg1] [msg2] [msg3] [msg4]
              off=0   off=1   off=2   off=3   off=4

Consumer committed offset: 3
→ Consumer has processed up to msg2 (offset 2)
→ Next read will start at offset 3 (msg3)

If consumer restarts → reads from offset 3 (no messages lost, no duplicates
if exactly-once enabled)
```

## Replication for Fault Tolerance

```
Partition 0, replication-factor=3:
  Leader:   Broker 1 (reads and writes go here)
  Follower: Broker 2 (replicates from leader)
  Follower: Broker 3 (replicates from leader)

If Broker 1 fails:
  Zookeeper/KRaft elects Broker 2 or 3 as new leader
  Producers/consumers reconnect to new leader automatically
```

speakable_v2.hook: Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform.
speakable_v2.cap: Adding a fourth consumer leaves one idle — you can't have more active consumers than partitions.

questions.title: Kafka Producers — Delivery Guarantees
questions.question: How do Kafka producer configurations affect delivery guarantees and throughput?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- acks=0: fire and forget — fastest, can lose messages
- acks=1: leader acknowledges — fast, loses messages if leader fails before replication
- acks=all (acks=-1): all ISR replicas acknowledge — slowest, no data loss
- idempotent producer: enable.idempotence=true — prevents duplicate delivery on retry
- Transactions: atomic writes across multiple partitions/topics
- Batching: batch.size and linger.ms — trade latency for throughput
- Compression: gzip, snappy, lz4 — reduces network/disk usage
- retries and retry.backoff.ms: automatic retry on transient failures

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Producer configuration is fundamentally about choosing between latency, throughput, and durability. The acks setting is the most critical choice. With acks=0, the producer sends and doesn't wait for any acknowledgment — maximum throughput but you can lose messages if the broker crashes before writing. With acks=1, the leader broker acknowledges after writing to its log — a good middle ground. With acks=all, every in-sync replica must acknowledge before the producer considers the write successful — maximum durability.

For critical data where losing even one message is unacceptable, combine acks=all with enable.idempotence=true. Idempotent producers get a unique producer ID and sequence numbers on each message, so the broker can detect and deduplicate retried messages. Without this, a network timeout causes the producer to retry a message that was already written, resulting in a duplicate.

Batching trades latency for throughput. linger.ms tells the producer to wait up to N milliseconds before sending a batch, accumulating more records. With linger.ms=5, requests that arrive within 5ms of each other are batched together and sent as one request — significantly improving throughput at the cost of slightly higher latency.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Producer configuration is fundamentally about choosing between latency, throughput, and durability.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: With linger.ms=5, requests that arrive within 5ms of each other are batched together and sent as one request — significantly improving throughput at the cost of slightly higher latency.

questions.title: Kafka Consumers and Consumer Groups
questions.question: How do Kafka consumers work, what is rebalancing, and how do you handle consumer failures?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Consumer Group: multiple consumers sharing partitions — each partition to one consumer
- Offset commit: tells Kafka which records have been processed — auto-commit vs manual
- auto.offset.reset: where to start reading when no committed offset (earliest vs latest)
- Rebalancing: triggered by consumer join/leave — partition reassignment, pauses consumption briefly
- Heartbeat: consumer sends heartbeat to indicate liveness; missed heartbeat triggers rebalance
- session.timeout.ms and max.poll.interval.ms: tune for slow processing
- Manual commit: commitSync() or commitAsync() — after successful processing
- Dead Letter Topic: failed messages routed to DLT for investigation

sections.Title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Consumer groups distribute work across multiple consumer instances. Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group, so adding consumers scales processing up to the number of partitions. When a consumer leaves the group — crash, restart, scale-down — Kafka triggers a rebalance where partitions are redistributed among the remaining consumers. During a rebalance, consumption pauses briefly.

Offset management is critical for exactly-once-or-at-least-once processing. With auto-commit, Kafka automatically commits offsets every 5 seconds. If the application processes a message and crashes before the next auto-commit, those messages are reprocessed after restart — at-least-once semantics. If you commit before fully processing, a crash means lost messages — at-most-once.

For at-least-once semantics, use manual commit: commit the offset only after successfully processing the message. Your processing must be idempotent to handle reprocessing safely. max.poll.interval.ms is important — if your consumer takes longer than this to call poll() again, Kafka assumes it's dead and triggers a rebalance. Increase it if your processing is inherently slow.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Consumer groups distribute work across multiple consumer instances.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Increase it if your processing is inherently slow.

questions.title: Kafka Topics, Partitions and Ordering
questions.question: How do you design Kafka topics and choose partition counts for a Java application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Partition count: determines max parallelism — more partitions = more consumers possible
- Key design: records with same key always go to same partition — ordering guarantee
- Partition key: use entity ID (orderId, userId) for natural ordering grouping
- Replication factor: typically 3 in production — tolerates 2 broker failures
- min.insync.replicas: minimum replicas that must ack for write to succeed (usually 2)
- Topic naming: use domain-event naming (orders.created, payments.processed)
- Compaction: log compaction keeps latest value per key — good for state tables

sections.Title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Partition count directly controls your maximum parallelism. If a topic has 6 partitions, you can have at most 6 active consumers in a consumer group processing it in parallel. Plan for future growth — you can increase partitions later but it affects key-to-partition mapping, potentially reordering existing events.

The partition key is how you guarantee ordering for related events. If you produce all events for a given order with the order ID as the key, Kafka's default partitioner consistently maps that order ID to the same partition. All events for that order are in that partition, and within a partition, ordering is strictly preserved. Without a consistent key, related events can land in different partitions and be processed out of order.

A common topic design guideline is one topic per event type — orders.created, orders.shipped, orders.cancelled — rather than one topic for all order events. This gives each consumer group the granularity to subscribe to only what it needs, and partition sizing can be tuned per event volume.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Partition count directly controls your maximum parallelism.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This gives each consumer group the granularity to subscribe to only what it needs, and partition sizing can be tuned per event volume.

questions.title: Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS — When to Use Each
questions.question: When would you choose Kafka over RabbitMQ or AWS SQS for messaging in a Java backend?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Kafka: event log, replay, high throughput (millions/sec), multiple consumers, long retention
- RabbitMQ: complex routing, messages deleted after consumption, per-message TTL, AMQP
- SQS: managed, no ops, AWS native, simple queue, at-least-once, max 14-day retention
- Use Kafka for: event sourcing, audit log, data pipelines, microservice event bus
- Use RabbitMQ for: task queues, complex routing rules, RPC patterns, smaller scale
- Use SQS for: AWS workloads, simple decoupling, no infrastructure management
- Throughput: Kafka >> SQS > RabbitMQ

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The fundamental difference is how they handle message storage. RabbitMQ and SQS delete messages after successful consumption — they're pure queues where a message exists until someone processes it. Kafka retains messages for a configured period regardless of whether they've been consumed, and consumers track their own position in the log.

Choose Kafka when you need message replay, multiple independent consumer groups reading the same events, or high throughput at millions of messages per second. The event sourcing pattern — storing every state change as an event and rebuilding state by replaying — requires Kafka's retention and replay capabilities. If a new service is deployed that needs to process historical events, it can start from the beginning of the topic.

Choose SQS when you're fully on AWS and want zero infrastructure management. SQS is managed, scales automatically, and integrates with all AWS services. It's the right choice for simpler decoupling scenarios — a web server offloading a task to a worker — where you don't need replay or multiple consumers.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Decision Matrix

| Requirement | Kafka | RabbitMQ | SQS |
|-------------|-------|----------|-----|
| High throughput (millions/sec) | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Message replay / history | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Multiple independent consumers | ✅ | Partial | ❌ |
| Complex routing | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Message TTL per message | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Managed (no ops) | ❌ (managed cloud options) | ❌ | ✅ |
| AWS native integration | MSK | ❌ | ✅ |
| Ordering guarantee | Per partition | Per queue | FIFO queue |
| Max retention | Unlimited | Until consumed | 14 days |

## Practical Examples

```
Kafka: E-commerce order event bus
├── Order service publishes: orders.created, orders.updated
├── Inventory service: consumer group #1 (reserves stock)
├── Notification service: consumer group #2 (emails)
├── Analytics service: consumer group #3 (dashboards)
└── Audit service: consumer group #4 (compliance, replays 1 year)

RabbitMQ: Email task queue
├── Exchange: topic exchange
├── Queue: email.transactional (routing key: email.send.tx)
├── Queue: email.marketing (routing key: email.send.mkt)
└── Each queue: one consumer, message deleted on ack

SQS: Image resize pipeline (AWS)
├── S3 upload event → SQS queue
├── Lambda consumers → resize to thumbnails
└── DLQ: failed resizes for investigation
```

speakable_v2.hook: The fundamental difference is how they handle message storage.

beats.text: I'd rethink this if the requirements changed significantly.

speakable_v2.cap: It's the right choice for simpler decoupling scenarios — a web server offloading a task to a worker — where you don't need replay or multiple consumers.

questions.title: Kafka Replication and Durability
questions.question: How does Kafka replication work and what configuration ensures message durability?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Replication factor: number of copies of each partition (3 for production)
- Leader: partition that handles all reads and writes
- Followers: replicate from leader; take over if leader fails
- ISR (In-Sync Replicas): replicas caught up to leader; acks=all uses ISR for acknowledgment
- acks=0: fire and forget — no guarantee
- acks=1: leader acknowledges — leader crash = message loss
- acks=all: all ISR acknowledge — survives broker failure
- min.insync.replicas=2: minimum replicas in ISR for produce to succeed
- Unclean leader election: allow non-ISR to become leader (data loss) — disable in production

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Kafka replication is how it achieves fault tolerance. Each partition has a leader and zero or more followers. The leader handles all reads and writes. Followers replicate the leader's log and stay in sync — these are called In-Sync Replicas or ISR. If the leader fails, Kafka elects one of the ISR followers as the new leader automatically.

The durability guarantee is controlled by two settings: acks on the producer and min.insync.replicas on the broker. With acks=all, the producer waits for all ISR to acknowledge before considering a send successful. With min.insync.replicas=2, at least 2 replicas must be in sync for the produce to succeed. Together, these ensure that even if one broker fails immediately after acknowledgment, the message exists on at least one surviving broker.

Unclean leader election is a critical setting to disable in production. If all ISR are unavailable and only a lagging follower is available, Kafka can elect it as leader — but it may be missing recent messages. This trades consistency for availability. In production, it's better to let the topic become temporarily unavailable than to silently lose data.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Replication Architecture

```
Topic: orders, Partition 0, Replication Factor: 3

Broker 1 (Leader):    [msg1][msg2][msg3][msg4]  ← receives all writes
Broker 2 (Follower):  [msg1][msg2][msg3]         ← replicating, 1 message behind
Broker 3 (Follower):  [msg1][msg2][msg3][msg4]  ← fully in sync

ISR = {Broker1, Broker3}  (Broker2 is lagging, removed from ISR)

With acks=all + min.insync.replicas=2:
  → msg4 acked to producer ✓ (Broker1 + Broker3 both have it)

Broker1 crashes → Broker3 elected as new leader
  → msg4 preserved ✓ (Broker3 had it)
```

## Durability Configuration

```yaml
# Producer
spring:
  kafka:
    producer:
      acks: all              # wait for all ISR
      retries: 10            # retry on transient failures
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true           # deduplicate retried messages
        max.in.flight.requests.per.connection: 5  # required for idempotence
        delivery.timeout.ms: 120000        # 2min total delivery timeout
        request.timeout.ms: 30000         # 30s per request
```

```bash
# Broker/Topic configuration
# Disable unclean leader election — never elect non-ISR broker
unclean.leader.election.enable=false

# Per-topic config
kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 \
  --entity-type topics \
  --entity-name orders \
  --alter \
  --add-config \
  min.insync.replicas=2,unclean.leader.election.enable=false,\
  replication.factor=3
```

## Availability vs Durability Trade-off

```
Scenario: 3 brokers, replication=3, min.insync.replicas=2

1 broker down:
  ISR = {B1, B3} → still 2 ISR → produces succeed ✓ (available + durable)

2 brokers down:
  ISR = {B1} → only 1 ISR, less than min.insync.replicas=2
  → NotEnoughReplicasException → produces FAIL
  Trade-off: prefer UNAVAILABILITY over data loss

With min.insync.replicas=1:
  → 2 brokers down: still accepts writes to single replica
  → 3rd broker down: data loss possible
  Use only when availability > durability (e.g., metrics, logs)
```

speakable_v2.hook: Kafka replication is how it achieves fault tolerance.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: In production, it's better to let the topic become temporarily unavailable than to silently lose data.
